title: How the microwave oven and Velcro were invented (Percy Spencer, George de Mestral)

sources.publisher: Lemelson-MIT Program, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
sources.title: Percy Spencer: Microwave Oven

sources.publisher: Lemelson-MIT Program, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
sources.title: George de Mestral: Velcro

facts.text: Percy Spencer was born in 1894 in Howland, Maine, in the United States.
During World War II, Spencer worked at the company Raytheon, which produced large amounts of radar equipment.
The magnetron, a machine used in radar, produces microwaves; Spencer did not invent it but found a way to mass-produce it.
While standing near a magnetron in a Raytheon lab, Spencer noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had begun to melt.
Spencer then held unpopped popcorn kernels near a magnetron, and the kernels popped.
Spencer filed for a patent on the microwave oven on October 8, 1945; it was granted in 1950.
Raytheon's first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, went on the market in 1947.
The first Radarange stood about 6 feet tall, weighed about 750 pounds and cost about 3,000 US dollars.
It took about 20 years before a smaller, more convenient microwave oven was ready for home use.
George de Mestral was born in Switzerland in 1907 and earned a degree in electrical engineering.
After a hike with his dog, de Mestral found burrs, a kind of plant seed, stuck to his clothes and his dog's fur.
Under a microscope, de Mestral saw that burrs have tiny hooks that catch on loops in cloth or animal fur.
De Mestral designed a fastener with one side of small hooks and one side of tiny loops.
His first attempts did not work well; he worked with a weaver in France and found that nylon worked best.
De Mestral perfected and patented the hook-and-loop design in 1955.
The name Velcro comes from the French words velours (velvet) and crochet (hook).
Velcro is used on clothing, shoes, bags and luggage, and NASA has used it to hold objects in place on space missions.
